headline: pki.transport reports the RFC 9266 tls-exporter channel binding of a TLS 1.3 connection, so every connection the toolkit opens now carries the binding its protocol version defines.
summary: The shared node:https transport adds tls.tlsExporter alongside protocol, cipher, peerCertificate, and tlsUnique, on both the response and the request body callback. It is the RFC 9266 binding: 32 bytes exported under the label EXPORTER-Channel-Binding with a zero-length context, the value both ends of the connection derive independently. It pairs with the tls-unique already reported for TLS 1.2, so the two are complementary rather than alternatives, and a caller reads whichever binding the negotiated version defines: tlsUnique below TLS 1.3, tlsExporter on TLS 1.3, each null on the version that does not define it. On TLS 1.2 and below tlsExporter is withheld rather than offered, because RFC 9266 sec. 2 defines the binding there only when the RFC 7627 extended master secret was negotiated, and Node exposes no way to confirm that; a socket that cannot export yields null as well, without failing the request. No shipped verb consumes tls-exporter: RFC 7030 sec. 3.5 binds tls-unique specifically, so a tls-exporter value does not belong in that challenge-password, and wiring it into an enrollment awaits a published EST-over-TLS-1.3 channel-binding profile.

Added: pki.transport.https reports tls.tlsExporter, the RFC 9266 channel binding of a TLS 1.3 connection (32 bytes, label EXPORTER-Channel-Binding, zero-length context), on its response and on the argument passed to a request body given as a function. It is null below TLS 1.3, where RFC 9266 sec. 2 also requires the RFC 7627 extended master secret that Node cannot confirm, and null when the socket cannot export. tls.tlsUnique is unchanged, so a connection carries exactly the binding its version defines.
